item.title: MRI-Driven Dual-Energy CT Synthesis via Conditional Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Models for MRI-only Radiotherapy and Protontherapy
item.description: arXiv:2611.28294v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) provides excellent soft-tissue contrast without ionizing radiation but lacks the electron-density information needed for radiotherapy dose calculation. Dual-energy computed tomography (DECT) improves tissue characterization and stopping-power ratio (SPR) estimation for proton therapy, but requires additional radiation exposure. We developed a denoising diffusion probabilistic model (DDPM) to synthesize high- and low-energy CT (sHECT and sLECT) simultaneously from a single MRI scan. Retrospective paired MRI-DECT data from patients receiving head-and-neck proton therapy were used to train and evaluate a multi-decoder DDPM with SwinViT or ResUNet denoisers. Performance was compared with Pix2PixGAN and CycleGAN using image-quality metrics, Hounsfield unit (HU) errors, anatomical profiles, and SPR maps and uncertainties. The DDPM outperformed both generative adversarial network baselines in visual fidelity and quantitative image quality. For sHECT and sLECT, respectively, mean absolute errors were 36.29 +/- 5.25 and 43.72 +/- 6.77 HU; peak signal-to-noise ratios were 27.44 +/- 1.06 and 26.26 +/- 0.98 dB; structural similarity indices were 0.89 +/- 0.02 and 0.87 +/- 0.03; and normalized cross-correlations were 0.95 +/- 0.01 and 0.94 +/- 0.01. The synthesized images preserved anatomical boundaries, while uncertainties in derived SPR maps remained within the expected acceptable range. MRI-based DECT synthesis using DDPM may provide tissue-specific information for proton therapy planning while reducing the need for radiation-based DECT acquisition.

item.title: A scalar arterial input function does not uniquely determine the perfusion residue: Theory and phantom MRI
item.description: arXiv:2611.28378v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Purpose: To relate the residue function of tracer kinetic models to blood velocity and cross-sectional tracer distributions at the arterial inlet, and show that a cross-sectionally averaged arterial input function (AIF) does not uniquely determine the residue. Theory and Methods: For steady laminar flow without radial diffusion, the residue function referenced to the cross-sectionally averaged inlet AIF was analytically derived from the velocity and inlet tracer distributions. In a straight tube with parabolic flow, two nonnegative inlet profiles sharing one measured AIF were compared for gamma-variate and rectangular arterial spin labeling (ASL) inputs. A straight-tube phantom was imaged at 3 T during gadolinium bolus passage, with uniform fills as controls. Results: In the phantom, enhancement during bolus arrival was greater near the lumen center than near the wall at all 11 stations and for all three boluses, whereas uniform gadolinium fills showed no such pattern. In the tube model, the two profiles produced tissue curves differing by up to 23.3% of the uniform-inlet peak and 0.30 s in time to peak for the gamma-variate input, and by 33.3% for ASL labels shorter than the fastest transit time. Their residues differed in initial amplitude and normalized temporal shape. Conclusion: Identical AIFs can produce different tissue concentration curves, depending on the spatial distributions of inlet tracer concentration and arterial flow velocity. Consequently, the residue-AIF tracer kinetic models may not be consistent with fluid mechanics or interpreted as tissue flow.

item.title: High-Resolution 3D Micro-CT Database of Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation (TMS) Coils for More Accurate Modelling, Technology Benchmarking, and Progress in Coil Design
item.description: arXiv:2611.29051v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Accurate modelling of transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) coils requires coil-specific geometric and electrical parameters. Yet detailed manufacturer models are rarely available, and internals may be widely available to companies in the field but not to researchers. The development of new coils should ideally build on all existing prior art. This work presents a technology benchmark and modelling-ready dataset for seventeen widely used commercial TMS coils across multiple manufacturers and geometries. High-resolution micro-CT (0.0495 mm resolution, material and density contrast) serves to reconstruct winding and casing structures and to extract parameters directly usable in numerical models, including loop dimensions, conductor cross-section, turn count, winding height, and winding-to-surface (casing) thickness. Complementary electrical measurements provide spectral impedance (series resistance and inductance) scans from 20 Hz to 200 kHz, together with dc resistance. In addition to baseline geometry and impedance, the study documents practical construction features relevant to safety and usability with detailed insights into their internal construction (e.g., cooling architectures and embedded sensing). The resulting benchmark dataset supports coil-specific electric-field simulations, reduces modelling uncertainty associated with generic assumptions (e.g., fixed coil-scalp spacing), and provides a quantitative reference for designing and evaluating new coil technologies against established commercial solutions. As a simulation-readiness example, we generated a calibrated CT-derived MCB70 line-current model for SimNIBS and evaluated its effect on predicted electric-field metrics. Compared with the SimNIBS MCB70 model, the CT-derived model produced measurable differences under identical placement conditions. We provide the dataset online.
item.dc:creator: Maryam Farahmandrad, Max Koehler, Mahdi Bayati, Denis Goldnik, Sergiy Antonyuk, Stephan Goetz

item.title: MRI Acquisition Parameters Influence Magnetic Resonance Hydrophone Measurements
item.description: arXiv:2611.29108v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Purpose:} To characterize the accuracy and precision of magnetic resonance hydrophone (MRH) measurements in response to changes in MR acquisition parameters. \textbf{Methods:} A human compatible MRH coil was coupled to a 500 kHz ultrasound transducer in a gel phantom. MRH acquisitions were repeated in a 3T scanner while altering in-plane resolution, slice thickness, encoding time, and device orientation within the MRI bore. The average and standard deviation of acoustic pressure estimates within a ROI near the encoding coil were compared to that obtained from the same transducer using a calibrated hydrophone in a water tank. The accuracy and precision of MRH scans, as well as a maximum detection depth, were then estimated. \textbf{Results:} Under high signal-to-noise (SNR) conditions, the MRH average pressure corresponded closely to those obtained by the hydrophone with no consistent measurement bias. However, too large or too small of voxel dimensions produced measurement underestimation, as expected by theory. Rotations as small as 15$^\circ$ out of alignment with the MRI bore also produced larger measurement underestimation than predicted by a dipole model of the encoding gradient coil. Increasing encoding times improved measurement precision but to a degree less than expected by theory. \textbf{Conclusion:} MR acquisition parameters exert a strong influence on MRH measurement accuracy and precision.
item.dc:creator: Hunter Harris, Ethan Bryan, Nathan Thyberg, Spencer Greding, Hyrum Mangum, Katia Oler, Davi Cavinatto, Taylor Webb, Steven Allen

item.title: Diffusion Posterior Sampling for Mitigation of Spatially-Variant System Blur in Ultra-High-Resolution CT of Trabecular Bone
item.description: arXiv:2611.29219v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Objective: CT spatial resolution degrades with distance from isocenter. We evaluate diffusion posterior sampling (DPS) deblurring for restoring structural detail and harmonizing texture features (TFs) of off-center trabecular bone to isocenter in ultra-high resolution CT (UHR CT). Methods: DPS pairs a diffusion prior, trained on isocenter UHR CT patches of trabecular bone from four human femora, with a likelihood term enforcing consistency with the observed image. Two variants were tested on a held-out femur at radial shifts of 90, 130 and 160 mm: KnownBlurDPS, with an anisotropic Gaussian kernel derived from modulation transfer function measurements, and BlindDPS, which estimated the kernel jointly with the image. Restored patches were compared with isocenter ground truth by structural similarity (SSIM), gradient magnitude similarity deviation (GMSD), and concordance correlation coefficient (CCC) of 40 gray-level co-occurrence and run-length TFs. Results: Both DPS variants improved SSIM and GMSD by 1-10% and mean TF CCC by 30-130%. The number of reproducible TFs (CCC > 0.80) at 90/130/160 mm rose from 13/2/1 without deblurring to 33/35/29 (KnownBlurDPS) and 40/36/16 (BlindDPS). At 90 mm, the accuracy of a linear classifier predicting the shift from TFs dropped from 79% to chance level with BlindDPS. Conclusion: DPS partly restores trabecular detail and TF reproducibility lost to spatially-variant blur in UHR CT; the blind variant matches the measured-kernel variant up to 130 mm. Significance: DPS deblurring can standardize trabecular bone TFs against patient mis-centering, potentially improving the robustness of TF-based CT radiomics; its blind form needs no CT system characterization.
item.dc:creator: T. Ye, G. Shi, A. Sivakumar, F. J. Quevedo Gonzalez, K. F. Moseley, J. A. Carrino, J. H. Siewerdsen, W. Zbijewski

item.title: High-Receiver-Bandwidth MRI Near Metal Implants with Motion-Consistent Rep2Rep Denoising
item.description: arXiv:2611.31003v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Purpose: To develop and evaluate a self-supervised denoising approach using motion-consistent Rep2Rep learning to enable high-receiver-bandwidth MRI for reduced metal-induced distortion. Methods: Motion-consistent Rep2Rep generates anatomically consistent training repetitions in the presence of inter-repetition motion by combining two acquired repetitions and splitting the combined k-space along the readout direction. The model was trained on 134 clinical low-receiver-bandwidth (300 Hz/pixel) MRI datasets and applied to 59 high-receiver-bandwidth (1028 Hz/pixel) MRI datasets. Three musculoskeletal radiologists independently scored low- and high-receiver-bandwidth images (before and after denoising) in a blinded manner for metal artifact reduction, image sharpness, perceived SNR, and overall image quality. A separate blinded reader preference evaluation was performed to compare motion-consistent Rep2Rep with standard Rep2Rep. Results: High-receiver-bandwidth MRI significantly reduced metal-induced artifact, while motion-consistent Rep2Rep improved perceived SNR and overall image quality. Compared to clinical low-receiver-bandwidth MRI, denoised high-receiver-bandwidth MRI achieved significantly higher metal artifact reduction scores (sagittal: 3.69 vs 3.01; axial: 3.83 vs 3.05; both P<0.0001) and comparable overall image quality scores (sagittal: 4.03 vs 3.98, P = 0.5391; axial: 3.95 vs 3.87, P=0.1266). The high-receiver-bandwidth axial protocol also reduced acquisition time by 47%. Motion-consistent Rep2Rep better preserved fine anatomical details than standard Rep2Rep. Conclusion: High-receiver-bandwidth MRI with motion-consistent self-supervised Rep2Rep denoising reduces metal-induced artifact without requiring dedicated high-receiver-bandwidth training data. This offers a practical approach for MRI near metal implants, such as postoperative cervical spine imaging.
item.dc:creator: Iman Khodarahmi, Renqing Luo, Nikola Janju\v{s}evi\'c, Christopher J Burke, Shana G Neumann, Yao Wang, Li Feng

item.title: Multi-Sensor Fusion for False-Alarm Reduction by Timed Electromechanical Corroboration
item.description: arXiv:2611.29025v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: A physician checks the clinical electrocardiogram against other observations. A wearable monitor has no physician. This paper shows that a mechanical sensor worn beside the electrocardiogram can take over that check, and that the right added sensors lower false alarms further. A beat is accepted only when a mechanical contraction follows at the delay learned for the wearer. Beat-shaped artifacts injected into resting and exercise recordings passed the electrocardiogram alone almost every time. A seismocardiogram or phonocardiogram as the second channel rejected most while keeping nearly all true beats, strongly at rest and partly during exercise. Shifting the mechanical signal in time removed the benefit. A detection criterion scores an added sensor by the part of its response that the sensors in place cannot predict. With four sensors, this score ranked the sets as their measured false-alarm rates did. With the two sensors it selected, 6.2 percent of the artifacts passed while 95 percent of true beats were kept, half the rate of the best single sensor. In integer arithmetic on a low-cost microcontroller, the detector made the same decisions as the software. These rates come from injected artifacts, not alarms in patients. Natural motion and clinical events remain untested.
item.dc:creator: Zixuan Fu, Anthony Raffaele, Unnikrishna Pillai

item.title: Comparison of Proton, Helium-Ion, and Carbon-Ion CT Imaging for Hadron Radiotherapy Using Monte Carlo Simulations
item.description: arXiv:2605.29593v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Objective: To perform a comprehensive comparative analysis of proton, helium-ion, and carbon-ion computed tomography (CT) as direct imaging modalities for hadron therapy treatment planning, focusing on Relative Stopping Power (RSP) reconstruction accuracy and patient radiation dose. Approach: High-fidelity Monte Carlo simulations were conducted using the GATE/Geant4 platform to model a standard CTP404 phantom. RSP maps were reconstructed using two iterative algorithms: the Simultaneous Algebraic Reconstruction Technique (SART) and the Richardson-Lucy (RL) deconvolution. Imaging performance was evaluated by comparing reconstructed RSP values against ground truth data for various tissue-equivalent inserts, while integral doses were estimated for a human head geometry using a Shepp-Logan-like phantom. Main results: All investigated particle modalities demonstrated a significant dose reduction compared to conventional X-ray CT protocols (which are approximately 40 mGy). The estimated imaging doses were 0.5 mGy for protons, 1.3 mGy for helium ions, and 7.5 mGy for carbon ions. In terms of accuracy, carbon-ion imaging achieved promising accuracy for soft-tissue materials (mean absolute error <0.5%). Helium ions offered a balanced performance with sub-1% errors for most materials and a dose burden significantly lower than carbon ions. Protons exhibited the widest range of RSP deviations. Significance: Direct particle imaging eliminates the systematic uncertainties inherent in photon-to-hadron conversion, which typically introduce RSP deviations of 1.6%-3.5% in standard single-energy X-ray CT. While carbon ions provide better RSP reconstruction precision essential for complex treatment plans in heterogeneous anatomy, helium and proton imaging offer exceptional dose sparing, making them particularly advantageous for pediatric patients and frequent adaptive replanning scenarios.
item.dc:creator: Zs\'ofia J\'olesz, G\'abor B\'ir\'o, G\'abor Papp, Gergely G\'abor Barnaf\"oldi

item.title: Depth-multiplexing spectral domain OCT for full eye length imaging with a single modulation unit
item.description: arXiv:2311.17824v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Clinical measurement of a patient's axial eye length is emerging as a crucial approach to track progression and monitor management of myopia. However, the preferred method for such measurements is swept-source OCT, whose cost prohibits broad use, especially in lower-income communities. Spectral domain (SD) OCT is a more affordable option, but it has limited imaging depth range, so is not suitable for full eye length measurement. Depth-multiplexing (DM) techniques for SD-OCT provide a workaround by capturing images at multiple depths within the eye. However, these methods typically require multiple light modulation units or detectors for simultaneous imaging across depths, adding complexity and cost. In response, we propose a novel DM-SD-OCT approach that utilizes a single light modulation unit for depth encoding. We capture images at multiple depths within the eye simultaneously with a single line scan camera, then computationally demix the contributions from different depths. Here, we demonstrate acquisition and demixing of signals from three distinct depths within the eye and validate experimentally in human subjects. Our method thus offers a cost-effective solution for comprehensive eye length measurement in clinical myopia research.
item.dc:creator: Xue Dong, Aster Zhang, Fabio Feroldi, Sarah Singh, Austin Roorda, Laura Waller, Guanghan Meng

item.title: Beam Geometry and Input Dimensionality: Impact on Sparse-Sampling Artifact Correction for Clinical CT with U-Nets
item.description: arXiv:2508.17961v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: This study aims to investigate the effect of various beam geometries and dimensions of input data on the sparse-sampling streak artifact correction task with U-Nets for clinical CT scans as a means of incorporating the volumetric context into artifact reduction tasks to improve model performance. A total of 22 subjects were retrospectively selected (01.2016-12.2018) from the Technical University of Munich's research hospital, TUM Klinikum rechts der Isar. Sparsely-sampled CT volumes were simulated with the Astra toolbox for parallel, fan, and cone beam geometries. 2048 views were taken as full-view scans. 2D and 3D U-Nets were trained and validated on 14, and tested on 8 subjects, respectively. For the dimensionality study, in addition to the 512x512 2D CT images, the CT scans were further pre-processed to generate a so-called '2.5D', and 3D data: Each CT volume was divided into 64x64x64 voxel blocks. The 3D data refers to individual 64-voxel blocks. An axial, coronal, and sagittal cut through the center of each block resulted in three 64x64 2D patches that were rearranged as a single 64x64x3 image, proposed as 2.5D data. Model performance was assessed with the mean squared error (MSE) and structural similarity index measure (SSIM). For all geometries, the 2D U-Net trained on axial 2D slices results in the best MSE and SSIM values, outperforming the 2.5D and 3D input data dimensions.
item.dc:creator: Tina Dorosti, Johannes Thalhammer, Sebastian Peterhansl, Daniela Pfeiffer, Franz Pfeiffer, Florian Schaff

item.title: Physics-Based Learning of the Wave Speed Landscape in Complex Media
item.description: arXiv:2602.03281v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: The propagation of waves through complex, inhomogeneous media is a fundamental challenge across scales, from optics to geophysics. In such environments, the waves reflected by the medium are typically dominated by a random speckle pattern, a complex interference resulting from multiple scattering by fine-scale heterogeneities. While this speckle is traditionally viewed as a source of noise that blurs the medium's structure, it contains rich information about the underlying wave speed landscape. Here, we introduce a physics-based learning framework that reconstructs the velocity distribution from the reflection matrix of the medium. We show how the speckle wave-field can be exploited to probe the focusing quality, serving as an intrinsic guide star to evaluate the local consistency of the velocity model. By representing wave propagation as a differentiable multi-layer network, we leverage optimization tools to solve the inverse problem and infer the wave speed map. We validate this approach through ultrasound experiments in highly scattering tissue-mimicking phantoms and human breast tissues, demonstrating its potential for tumor detection and characterization where standard methods fail. This synergy between wave physics and gradient-based optimization provides a general paradigm for non-invasive tomography in any complex environment where reflection data is available.
item.dc:creator: Baptiste H\'eriard-Dubreuil, Emma Brenner, Benjamin Rio, William Lambert, Foucauld Chamming's, Mathias Fink, Alexandre Aubry
